title: Testing & Evaluating Agents
subtitle: It worked in the demo. Learn to grade an AI with a rubric. Then put a real coding agent to work, and grade what it builds.
heroTitle: Testing & Evaluating Agents

objectives.title: Tell a Vibe Check from a Test
objectives.description: Watch a demo go three for three, then see the message nobody tried. "It looked fine when I tried it" is not an answer.

objectives.title: Write a Rubric
objectives.description: A test case is one input plus what a good answer must do and must not do. Three kinds: everyday (happy path), tricky (edge case) and trap (adversarial test).

objectives.title: Put a Real Coding Agent to Work
objectives.description: Run OpenCode, an open-source coding agent, on a real task. See the tools, permissions and job description you learned this semester inside a real product.

objectives.title: Change One Thing and Check Again
objectives.description: Add one sentence to the agent's job description and rebuild. Count what you fixed and what you broke. The second one has a name: a regression.

agenda.title: Three Kinds of Question, One Rule
agenda.description: A good exam mixes everyday, tricky and trap questions.
bulletPoints: Grade what it does, not the words
🟢 everyday (happy path) · 🌀 tricky (edge case) · 🎭 trap (adversarial test)
Change one thing, then check everything again. 🔧 fixed, 💥 broke

bulletPoints: The rubric: week total, top dish, busiest day, a chart that matches. Must not: Pad Thai as the top dish

activities.title: Grade It
activities.description: Whole room, on your phone, about 9 minutes:

steps.title: Round 1: your gut (60 s)
steps.description: Ten AI answers from North End Noodle Co. Pass or fail? No rules, no answer key.

steps.title: Round 2: the rubric (2 min)
steps.description: The same ten answers, each with what the manager wrote down: what a good answer must do and must not do.

steps.title: Compare
steps.description: Your gut vs. the rubric. Which ones did you change your mind on, and why?

steps.title: Give it the mission
steps.description: Open Marco's folder and paste the mission. The agent reads sales.csv and builds report.html: totals, a chart, and three things Marco should do next week.

steps.title: Grade it
steps.description: Check the report against the rubric with sales.csv open next to it. One line is a trap: the biggest single row is Pad Thai on Saturday, but Ramen wins the week.

steps.title: Change one thing
steps.description: Write one sentence in AGENTS.md, the agent's job description. Ask it to rebuild. Grade again: 🔧 fixed or 💥 broke?

steps.title: Pick a real person
steps.description: A friend, a parent, your club. First names only, nothing private.

steps.title: Write the exam first
steps.description: Three things it must do and one thing it must not, all checkable with your eyes. The lab page turns them into a mission. The term: test-first.

steps.title: Build, grade, send
steps.description: The agent builds gift.html. Grade it against your own rubric. If it passes, send it to them.

activities.title: The Exam (over the break)
activities.description: A Colab notebook, about 35 minutes, on your class pass:

steps.title: The demo vs. the exam
steps.description: Your AI employee looks perfect on three messages. Then it takes an 8-question exam, graded by a second AI with a rubric.

steps.title: Fix it, then stump it
steps.description: Add one sentence and retake the whole exam. Then write the question it gets wrong, and ask it three times.

steps.title: Your agent's exam
steps.description: Three test cases for your own final project agent: everyday, tricky and trap.

takeaways.text: A demo is a highlight reel. An exam is the whole season. Three good answers that somebody picked is a vibe check. "6 of 8, and here is the one it fails" is an answer.
An exam tests what the business needs, not what you told the AI. The customer doesn't read your prompt. The person who knows the customer writes the questions, and that is a business job.
A test needs a rubric, and the rubric comes first. What must a good answer do, and what must it not do? Write it before you see the result, so you grade what you wanted and not what you got.
Change one thing, then check everything again. A fix that breaks something that used to work is a regression. You only see it if you check every line again.
A real coding agent is made of what you learned: tools, permissions, a job description. It built a report in minutes. Knowing whether the report is right was still your job.
